title: How do we find the missing numbers in a pattern?
description: Three number patterns with missing numbers are completed by finding the gap from each number to the next. One pattern has a steady gap, one is two patterns taking turns, and one has gaps that grow by one. The video breaks the slip of thinking every pattern needs the same gap each time.
teaching_notes: One idea: the gap from one number to the next, target minus start, shows the rule of a pattern. Watch for students who look for one steady gap in every sequence, or who only extend forwards when numbers are missing at the start.

video_script.why: The child completes three sequences by finding the gap between neighbours as target minus start, then repeating or extending it.
video_script.substitution: The book's three sequences, read as jumps on the number line using Target Position − Starting Position = Movement.
video_script.anchor: the three sequences of the book written as rows of boxes
video_script.payoff_line: The gaps between neighbours show the rule of each sequence

final_answer.spoken: minus sixteen, minus ten and minus four; minus one, eight and minus two; twenty seven, nineteen, minus eight, minus nine and minus nine

never_show: the missing numbers before their steps
maths_rules: b: odd places 3, 2, 1, 0 go down by 1, so the next is −1 and then −2; even places 4, 5, 6, 7 go up by 1, so the next is 8
c backwards: the gap into 12 is −7, so the number before it is 12 + 7 = 19; the gap into 19 is −8, so the first number is 19 + 8 = 27
video_script.design: Each sequence is a row of boxes with jump arrows between neighbours. The gap is written on every arrow, and the missing boxes fill in one by one.
